say.text: A 19-year-old with suspected appendicitis describes the course of his pain over 12 hours.
Which course is typical?

choices.label: Right lower belly from the start, and it never moves
Starts at the navel, then moves to the right lower belly
Right lower belly from the start, then spreads to the navel
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Early gut-wall pain travels by visceral fibres entering at T10. Which is vague and central, and which is pinpoint? Which comes first?
Constant right-sided pain is the picture most people remember from the clinic.
Think about the gut wall's own nerve supply, which reaches the cord at T10. Where would pain carried that way be felt, and could it be pinpoint?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so trace the course from the first hour, not from the clinic picture.

say.text: Pain that starts on the right and climbs is tempting, because right-sided pain is the one you remember.
Ask which pain the gut wall's visceral fibres carry first, and which pain needs the peritoneum to be inflamed.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so work out which nerves fire first before you choose a direction.

say.text: Yes. The pain starts periumbilical, from visceral afferents at T10.
It shifts to the right iliac fossa when the parietal peritoneum is involved.

choices.label: Skip the teaching, go to the blockage

say.text: Two regions, two nerve supplies. Visceral pain comes from the gut wall, enters at T10 and sits round the navel.
Somatic pain comes from the parietal peritoneum and is localised to the right iliac fossa.
Pain moves when the inflammation moves from the gut wall out to the peritoneum.
The pain localises to the right iliac fossa only after the early stage.
What causes that localisation?

choices.label: Rising lumen pressure stimulates the T10 visceral fibres more strongly
Wall ischaemia starts before the lumen blocks, so pain turns local
Inflammation reaches the parietal peritoneum, giving somatic pain
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Visceral fibres cannot pinpoint a spot. Which layer has to be inflamed before pain can point to one place?
Pressure is the first real change inside the lumen, so it feels like the cause of where the pain sits.
Pressure acts on the same nerves as the early pain. Can fibres that enter at T10 ever point to one spot?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so ask which structure can localise, not which event comes first.

say.text: Ischaemia is the dangerous event you remember, so it feels like it could come first.
Place it in the chain. Does the wall's blood supply fail before or after the lumen is blocked and the pressure builds?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so trace the chain from the lumen outward, not back from the gangrene.

say.text: Follow the chain from the lumen: obstruction, continued mucus, rising pressure, venous congestion. Only then does the arterial supply fail.
The pain localises when inflammation reaches the peritoneum, not when the lumen first blocks.
Think of a blocked drain: the water backs up first, and the pipe gives way at its weakest point.
Yes. Inflammation reaching the parietal peritoneum makes the pain somatic and localised to the right iliac fossa.
The appendicular artery is a branch of the ileocolic artery, and it runs in the mesoappendix.
It is an end artery: once it thromboses, gangrene follows, usually first at the antimesenteric border.
So thrombosis of this one artery leads straight to gangrene and perforation.
The appendicular artery thromboses. Which outcome follows, and why so fast?

choices.label: Gangrene and perforation, as no other artery can take over
Gangrene sets in first, then the lumen blocks, as ischaemia leads
Pressure rises only after the artery fails, as the artery leads
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: When this one artery clots, ask whether any other vessel can take over its supply, and what that means for how fast the wall dies.
Gangrene is the outcome you remember most, so it can feel like the opening act.
Gangrene is the end point of the story. Which event in the lumen sets the whole chain going?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so trace the chain from the lumen, not from the end picture.

say.text: The artery is what a surgeon worries about, so its failure can feel like the first event.
Think about which way the arrow runs: does the blocked lumen affect the artery, or the artery the lumen?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the direction of the arrow before you choose.

say.text: Yes. Because the appendicular artery is an end artery, its thrombosis gives gangrene and perforation with no backup.
Murphy's sequence describes the order of symptoms in typical appendicitis.
Which order is it?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Start with the first symptom the patient notices, then ask what the gut does after that, and what the body does last.
Vomiting is the symptom many patients mention first, so it feels like the opening act.
Ask which symptom the patient notices before the gut reacts at all.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so use the order as the clue, not the list.

say.text: Fever feels like the sign of infection, so it seems it should arrive early.
Think about how high the temperature usually runs, and whether it appears before or after the gut reacts with nausea.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so remember fever is the late sign.

say.text: Yes. Pain first, then vomiting, then a low-grade fever.
Pain comes first, from the gut wall stretching. Anorexia is almost constant, and nausea with a few vomits follows the onset of pain.
Fever comes last and is usually low-grade.
So a story where vomiting came first argues against appendicitis, and a high fever points to perforation.
A young adult vomited several times through the morning, then developed diffuse abdominal pain and loose stools.
Which reading fits best?

choices.label: Appendicitis likelier, since vomiting usually opens the illness
Gastroenteritis likelier, since diffuse pain rules out appendicitis
Gastroenteritis likelier, since vomiting came before the pain
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Find which symptom the story gives first, then ask which picture that order favours.
Vomiting is often the first symptom patients mention, so it feels like the opening act.
Compare the order in this story with the order of symptoms in appendicitis. What comes first in each?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so use the order as a filter.

say.text: Vague, widespread pain sounds like a gut infection rather than a surgical problem.
Recall where early appendicitis pain is felt and which nerves carry it. Does vague, central pain rule it out?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so ask what each clue really rules out.

say.text: Yes. Vomiting before pain points away from appendicitis, where the pain comes first.
A 9-year-old, recovering from a viral illness, develops right iliac fossa pain from a blocked appendix lumen.
What is the likeliest cause of the block?

choices.label: Swollen lymphoid tissue in the wall
A hard faecolith lodged in the lumen
Either, since age does not change the cause
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: How does the amount of lymphoid tissue in the appendix wall change from childhood to later life, and what does a viral illness do to it?
A faecolith is the textbook block, so it is tempting whenever obstruction comes up.
Check the age and the recent illness. Which tissue in the wall is plentiful at that age, and what does a viral infection do to it?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so read the age and the history in the stem before you pick a cause.

say.text: Both can block a lumen, so calling them equal feels fair.
Look at what the stem tells you about the patient. Does the commonest cause stay the same from childhood to adulthood?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so age is the cue before the cause.

say.text: Yes. A swollen lymphoid wall is the child's block, after viral infection.
The age in the stem decides the cause, so check it first.
In children the lymphoid tissue is maximal and swells after viral infection, so lymphoid hyperplasia blocks the lumen.
In adults the lymphoid tissue has atrophied, and a faecolith is the commonest block.
The age in the stem decides which block you are looking for.
A 45-year-old had a cold last week, and now has three days of right iliac fossa pain.
What is the commonest cause of the luminal block at this age?

choices.label: Swollen lymphoid tissue in the wall
A faecolith lodged in the lumen
Either, since age does not change the cause
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Go back to the age: the child's answer may not carry over. What hardens and collects in an older lumen?
The recent cold pulls you toward the child's answer, because it fits so well.
Check the age first. What has happened to the wall's lymphoid tissue by 45, and what usually collects in an adult lumen?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so let the age decide, not the history.

say.text: Age changed the answer for the child, and it can change it again here.
Which of the two causes belongs to adults?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check which way the age points.

say.text: Yes. In adults a faecolith is the commonest block, whatever the recent history.
